entries.title: ‘A Lot of Chaos’: How the Secretaries’ Cup Finally Arrived at Audi Field
entries.summary: The second half of an ambitious Saturday afternoon doubleheader, the Division III football game did not have an official start time until Thursday.
entries.content:
Trinity Rodman had barely landed her victory leap before the field crew at Audi Field rushed into action.

As a sold-out stadium of Washington Spirit fans roared in celebration of the club clinching its third straight trip to the NWSL championship match, the advertisements circling the field were covered up, and the soccer nets were taken down and replaced with football goalposts. Attendees clustered around the side of the field were shooed away by security a few minutes after the final whistle.

“Man,” said a dad corralling three young girls in matching pink puffer jackets. “They want us out of here.”

In two hours, Audi Field was transformed into a football venue for the Secretaries’ Cup, the annual NCAA Division III game between the U.S. Coast Guard Academy and U.S. Merchant Marine Academy.

But the path to Saturday's doubleheader was much longer than that changeover, and it had been filled with uncertainty.

The Secretaries’ Cup had long been scheduled for 1 p.m. on Saturday at Audi Field. But that was thrown into doubt after the Spirit qualified to host a playoff semifinal that same afternoon. The NWSL club is a full-time tenant of Audi Field but does not manage scheduling for the venue, which is handled by the primary tenant and operator, D.C. United. It originally seemed likely that Spirit leadership would need to secure a different venue for its semifinal, and so team executives began planning for a match at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Maryland.

But a flurry of last-minute dealmaking allowed the Spirit to preserve its home-field advantage at Audi. The move was partially underwritten by a sponsor, Lafayette Credit Union, whose executives were named honorary captains of the semifinal match. They received what surely must have been the biggest cheer any sponsor has ever gotten from the crowd as players and fans alike were thrilled to keep the game at “Rowdy Audi.”

But the switch left cadets, midshipmen, families and alumni wondering for days: What about the Secretaries’ Cup?

A new kickoff time for the game was not made public until Thursday morning. Sources familiar with the discussions said that federal government involvement with security and logistics prevented a new time from being announced sooner. Audi Field eventually announced plans for an ambitious doubleheader: NWSL soccer at 12 p.m. and NCAA football at 4:30 p.m., with lines painted on the playing surface for both games: soccer in yellow and football in white. The bases of the goalposts were installed with padding before the soccer match.

In the days before that announcement, fans had wondered if the game would be played later in the night, or at a different venue. Some began traveling to the game before they knew when or where it would kick off.

That group included Keith McLiverty, the president of the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy National Parents Association, who began driving to D.C. on Thursday before the new time had been announced.

“It’s just a lot of chaos,” McLiverty told The Washington Sun. “There’s people coming from all across the country for this game… It just shows disrespect to the tradition and to what the game stands for.”

Some expressed frustration at the game being dismissed as unimportant amid the scheduling chaos. A Merchant Marine alumnus said that it can feel like they are treated as the “red-headed stepchild of the academies.” Others noted this would likely never happen to any of the service academies who play in Division I.

One parent asked simply: “Would they do this to Army-Navy?”

The Secretaries’ Cup has been played annually for nearly 50 years. Historically, the game alternated between the campuses of the two academies, but it recently began using marquee venues at neutral sites — Fenway Park in Boston last year and Audi in D.C. this year. Washington was chosen as the 2026 site to include the game in celebrations for America250.

The game has come to serve as an annual gathering for cadets and midshipmen and their families. There are galas, dinners and parties scheduled around the contest, many of which hung in the balance as the schedule was in doubt.

Suzanne Hoffman from Melbourne, Florida, wore a “Marine Merchant Academy Mom” button on her jacket on Saturday. Her son is a midshipman, and the Secretaries’ Cup was her first time seeing him after he spent four months at sea, including time in the Strait of Hormuz as part of Operation Epic Fury.

“Coming to this game is a great way to support the kids that are going to fight for our country someday,” Hoffman said. “These are big games. Some kids look at their season being successful based on whether they beat the Coast Guard Academy.”

The new kickoff time (and the nationwide ground stop that happened the night before the game) did not stop Hoffman from getting to the Secretaries’ Cup. She expected flight delays would make her trip home less-than-pleasant. But for this, it was worth it, she said.

Some of the game’s pageantry had to be adjusted. A military flyover that had been in the works for months did not take place. A Coast Guard alumni party planned for after the game became a pregame affair. Just one of the two titular secretaries was in attendance for the coin toss, with Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin present, but not Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy.

But much of the frustration of the last few days fell away once the game began. For Steve Werner, a Baltimore native whose son-in-law played for the Merchant Marine Academy, a matchup against Coast Guard is guaranteed “fun football to watch,” no matter what.

“These guys put everything they have into it,” Werner said.

The Merchant Marines eventually romped to a 42-14 win. It took place a few hours later than originally scheduled and a little bit differently than planned. But it was still the game they loved.

“I was able to see so much support,” said Cat Saucier, who works for the U.S. Coast Guard Academy Alumni Association. “Everybody’s trying their best and doing what they can with what they have, and so far, what we have has been incredible.”
entries.author: Emma Baccellieri, Emma Ruby

entries.title: Flight Cancellations Continue as Trump Demands More Money and Blames Biden
entries.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said flights should be “running at full capacity” by Monday.
entries.content:
More than 1,600 cancellations and thousands of delays hit airlines Sunday, according to Flight Aware, while President Donald Trump broke his silence on the disruption to demand more funding from Congress and blame the Biden administration for the issues that caused the complete ground stop Friday.

“If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently. It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote Sunday on Truth Social. “Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!”

The president added that his administration has “already started the work” but Congress must provide additional funding to allow the modernization efforts to happen all at once.

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,” Trump wrote in a separate post to Truth Social on Sunday. “Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began.”

The president had not publicly addressed the ground stop, which was the second complete ground stop covering the entire U.S. airspace since the Sept. 11 attacks, until he posted Sunday. A pilot warning system failure prompted a 90-minute ground stop in 2023.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS’s “Face the Nation” that flights should return to “running at full capacity” by Monday.

Duffy took a more measured approach to assigning blame for the issues that led to Friday’s ground stop, arguing that a lack of decades of poor investment in modernizing the systems were at fault.

“I’m proud of the work we’re doing, the attention we’re bringing to this issue. But I can’t apologize for what was passed off to us,” Duffy said Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “And I can’t blame Republicans or Democrats because it’s all of them.”

In a press conference on Friday evening, Duffy called for $50 billion to replace the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging telecommunications system. Air traffic controllers have been relying on aging copper wire and routing systems, but the Trump administration has pushed to overhaul this technology by replacing it with fiber optic networks and satellites.

Trump’s “one big, beautiful bill” also designated $12.5 billion to modernize the air traffic control system. The FAA has described that $12.5 billion as a “down payment” and said in December 2025 that $20 billion more is needed for the Brand New Air Traffic Control System, also known as BNATCS.

Duffy told CNN’s “State of the Union” the FAA still needs more money because the $12.5 billion is “very specific” and said there is “no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom.”

Some Democratic lawmakers have questioned Duffy’s push for additional funding, criticising the Trump administration’s focus on controversial construction projects like the Triumphal Arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

“You’ve literally controlled Congress for the past two years. And apparently, there’s always been money for vanity projects. But none to fix our air traffic control system?” Sen. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, the top Democrat on the Senate Aviation Subcommittee wrote Friday on X. “Perhaps Trump should prioritize aviation safety over his pathetic Arch.”

Duffy announced over the weekend that the FAA is actively investigating how a contractor’s replacement of the copper wire may have caused the ground stop. Duffy explained that the maintenance caused the FAA’s network to be flooded with thousands of connection attempts every minute, which overloaded the system.

Duffy railed against the L3Harris, the telecommunications contractor, on Sunday as the FAA continues to investigate whether the issue can be attributed to technician error or faulty equipment.

“I want to get away from L3Harris and get to a new one, but they own the network, so I can't cancel the network that they own and I operate on,” Duffy said on “Meet the Press.”

The transportation secretary said he is asking for “billions of dollars from Congress to build a brand new architecture of a network by the best companies in the world, including AT&T, Verizon, and Lumens” — adding that the companies are “ready to deploy tomorrow” but the FAA needs “the money to tell them to start.”

Duffy and other administration officials like Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin have repeatedly said that they do not believe the U.S. had been targeted by any sort of cyber attack and had not been linked to the global Microsoft outage last week.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: No. 19 Maryland Rolls Past Columbia, 85-58
entries.summary: Sophomore Rainey Welson scored a career-high 17 points off the bench.
entries.content:
Rainey Welson scored a career-high 17 points off the bench to lead five players in double figures and No. 19 Maryland rode a dominating first half to an 85-58 victory over Columbia on Sunday.

Welson, a sophomore, made 5 of 8 3-pointers and both of her free throw attempts. Addi Mack scored 14 points and Bri McDaniel, Nunu Agara and Jordyn Jackson all scored 10 for the Terrapins (2-1).

The Terrapins shot 48% overall, making 10 of 17 3-pointers (59%) and 19 of 21 free throws (91%). They had 16 assists and scored 29 points following 23 Columbia turnovers.

Riley Weiss scored 13 points and Hilke Feldrappe 10 for the Lions (3-2).

Maryland scored the first 11 and the last nine points of the first quarter, building a 20-5 lead. The Terrapins forced eight turnovers, leading to 13 points.

A 13-0 run in the second quarter helped Maryland take a 41-14 lead at halftime.

Columbia fared better in the second half while Maryland's reserves got more playing time. The Terps had a 22-21 advantage in the third quarter and Columbia had the edge in the fourth, 23-22.
entries.author: The Associated Press
